rationale: The human Parkinson cohort gives an inconclusive, nonmonotonic association with binary hyposmia. Concentrated green-tea extract produced olfactory tissue lesions in mice without testing smell. The newer cell work measures survival, and the general-population study examined other teas. The direction of smell severity after brewed green tea in Parkinson remains unresolved.

A registered dormitory-room trial found lower global sleep-quality scores with sage tea than with its brown-sugar control. That oral common-sage result and menopause extract signals give a minimal lean toward improvement. A small primary-insomnia trial found an inconclusive comparison with active chamomile, and the Parkinson dried-leaf trial did not measure sleep. Preparation, sugar, clustering, reporting and population differences leave substantial uncertainty.

A randomized non-Parkinson comparison of extra-virgin with refined olive oil found a 4.22-point adjusted constipation difference favoring the extra-virgin grade. The registry and paper describe the same study and differ on written dosing. Parkinson whole-diet results and a dialysis active-control comparison were inconclusive. Topical massage and bundled ketogenic observations supply no isolated oral Parkinson effect. The grade and outcome still support a small favorable inference across populations.
